We thank the reviewer for their positive response and for these important clarifying questions. We are happy to provide the details as below and will update the manuscript accordingly.

**Q1. Definitions of $L_{train}$ and $A_{test}$:**

- **Training loss ($L_{train}$):** The training error is the **cross-entropy loss**, as mentioned in  Appendix A.1. We will add one more sentence in the final version to make it clearer. 

- **Smoothed test accuracy ($A_{test}$):** This is introduced in Section 3.3, where we employ a sigmoid function to approximate test accuracy and make it differentiable. This follows the implementation in Yang et al. 2025(see Ref [2]). To make it clear, we will add this citation to the definition in Section 3.3 and provide the implementation details in the appendix of the final version.

**Q2. Intuition for Sign in Eq. (7):** This is an excellent question and we thank the reviewer for it. The reviewer’s intuition is correct: the negative sign in the entropy gradient term acts as a ‘force’ to push the system towards **lower-entropy** regions. This is also the fundamental mechanism why WLMD can uniformly sample across all regions with different entropy. The key to resolving this seeming contradiction is that WanD applies this force **only along the 1D training loss (x-axis) direction**. 

As presented in Figure 1(a) and 1(b), there are two relatively higher entropy regions: the **high train loss regime** (when comparing along the x-axis) and the **high test accuracy regime** (when comparing along the y-axis). WanD has an ‘entropy force’ along the train loss direction (x-axis), pushing the model towards the **low train loss regime** (low entropy), as desired for an optimizer. There is **no entropy force** applied along the test accuracy (y-axis) direction, because WanD as an optimizer cannot access the test data directly. At a given train loss level, the model will naturally find the **high test accuracy regime** (high entropy), with a probability scaling with exp(entropy), because these solutions occupy a much larger volume in the parameter space.

This mechanism also explains WanD’s advantage in grokking resistance. For a grokking system, standard optimizers like AdamW get kinetically trapped by small gradients once the train loss is minimized and can only find the generalization state via the cumulation of many small stochastic updates during a long period of time (the "slow relaxation"). In contrast, the explicit ‘entropy force’ in WanD can guide the model towards high-volume, generalized solutions within the low train loss regime, therefore preventing grokking.

Thanks for the reviewer's prompt response and the crucial clarification. We had initially misinterpreted the reviewer's suggestion as evaluating WanD on tasks other than modular arithmetic (e.g., the MNIST dataset), which we considered out of the scope of this paper. We agree that testing on non-grokking modular arithmetic tasks can significantly strengthen our manuscript. 

According to prior work (Power et al. 2022, Liu et al. 2022), there are two popular methods to construct **non-grokking modular arithmetic tasks**: 1) increase the split fraction of training data (by default it is 50%); 2) constrain the weight norm in the ‘Goldilocks’ zone during training.  We chose to run experiments on the first setting, as this approach evaluates the optimizer's adaptability without introducing explicit regularization, which WanD is designed to be free of. We have run experiments on three increased training data split fractions: 70%, 75%, and 80%. We first verified that grokking is greatly reduced at 70% and 75%, and finally eliminated at 80% when training with AdamW. This is also consistent with results reported in Power, et al. In all three cases, WanD can generalize and find high weight norm generalizing solutions (test accuracy > 99%), similar to grokking tasks. We also find the WanD optimization trajectory becomes relatively more stable when grokking is eliminated (train fraction is 80%). We believe these results can demonstrate WanD’s applicability in non-grokking modular arithmetic tasks.

We are grateful for this suggestion as it has allowed us to demonstrate WanD’s applicability and robustness. We will add a new subsection with these results to the appendix of the final version.  In addition, we will also discuss our progress on the WanD-AdamW hybrid optimization approach, which can achieve the similar level of stability as AdamW but also eliminate grokking without any further modification.

We thank the reviewer for the encouraging comments on our work, especially on the originality of our physics-inspired idea. We also greatly appreciate the reviewer’s effort in sharing such a thorough and insightful list of questions, which helps us to further polish the manuscript. Due to the max length limit, we have provided concise responses for some points below, but we look forward to discussing any points in more detail during the discussion period.

$\textbf{Weakness}$

$\textbf{W1. Choice of binning size}$: Our choice of binning is a balance between computational cost and the resolution of the entropy landscape. According to previous numerical analysis for Wang-Landau methods ([Belardinelli et al., 2008, Analysis), the bin size determines the final resolution but does not alter the converged landscape qualitatively. We use the log scale for train loss to focus resolution on the low loss regime. 

$\textbf{W2. Main takeaway}$: Our primary contribution is a new physics-inspired mechanism for grokking, which goes beyond the general entropy-generalization correlation in Ref [2]:
- We show that grokking can be understood as a computational glass relaxation: a slow relaxation from a kinetically trapped, low-entropy, memorization state to a high-entropy generalization state.
- We provide counterexamples to the first-order phase transition and the weight norm determined hypotheses for grokking.
- Our WanD optimizer serves as a practical demonstration of our theory.

$\textbf{W3. WLMD convergence proof}$: The guaranteed convergence is a key reason why we choose the Wang-Landau method. We cited the reference of WLMD (Ref [29]) in the main text, which contains the detailed formula derivation process. We will add [Fort et al. 2015 Convergence] for mathematical proof.

$\textbf{W4. Different set up from Ref [1]}$: We chose to use the same setup as Ref [28] because it is the most standard one for grokking experiments (e.g. Refs [3, 10, 25]), focusing on $\textbf{delayed generalization after overfitting}$. In contrast, the setup and definition of grokking in Ref [1] is slightly different from the original grokking discovered in Ref [8]. It focuses more on the ‘sharp drop in test loss’ . Therefore, we believe the setup from Ref [28] is a more appropriate choice for our investigation. We agree that applying our analysis to other grokking-like phenomena, such as the one in Ref [1], is an important direction for future work.

$\textbf{Questions}$

$\textbf{Q1}$. In our analogy, the training loss ($L_{train}$) maps to the potential energy (U), as both are minimized during optimization. The test accuracy ($A_{test}$) does not map to energy. Instead, it serves as a macroscopic $\textbf{order parameter}$ measuring generalization.

$\textbf{Q2}$. Yes, the term $\partial S / \partial L_{train}$ is calculated via numerical differentiation of adjacent bins (see SL_grad() in our code). The reviewer is correct that the estimate is poor initially and this is a well-understood aspect of the Wang-Landau method. The algorithm is designed to automatically fix it over time by using the inaccurate estimates of the entropy to bias the sampling, forcing the simulation to explore the under-sampled regions. This guarantees the eventual convergence to the true entropy distribution (Ref [29] and [Fort et al., 2015]).

$\textbf{Q3}$. We thank the reviewer and will add algorithm boxes for both WLMD and WanD. 

$\textbf{Q4}$. While the reviewer's intuition is correct that controlling the kinetic energy stabilizes the simulation, the primary reason for its conservation is to satisfy the $\textbf{theoretical requirements}$ of the WLMD method. Since the system's temperature is directly proportional to its average kinetic energy and our goal is to sample the canonical ensemble at a constant temperature (WLMD convergence requirement), we must conserve it.

$\textbf{Q5}$. This is an excellent question and we thank the reviewer for it. Our primary evidence for concluding that grokking is not a first-order phase transition is the $\textbf{absence of a free-energy barrier}$ (see details in our response to Q6). The continuous nature of our chosen order parameter serves as complementary evidence. 

We believe the test accuracy is a good choice of order parameters because they are the most appropriate one to describe the macroscopic phenomenon of grokking. While it is theoretically possible to manually construct a discontinuous order parameter for networks during grokking, it would be an ill-suited one that fails to describe the process clearly. For example, we can define a binary parameter called ‘perfect generalization’, which is 1 only at 100% test accuracy and 0 otherwise. Such an order parameter is $\textbf{discontinuous by definition}$, but it is insufficient to describe how generalization evolves during grokking. 

$\textbf{Q6}$. Yes, the reviewer’s reasoning is correct on a high level. In physics, a first-order transition is defined by a $\textbf{discontinuity in the first derivative of the free energy}$, which is the ‘jump’ mentioned by the reviewer. 
The need to cross a free energy barrier implies first order transition because it indicates the existence of a $\textbf{thermodynamically unfavorable intermediate state}$ (like a nucleation seed in water freezing). This prevents a smooth, continuous transformation and forces the system to change discontinuously. 

$\textbf{Q7}$. The key is to distinguish between the $\textbf{training trajectory}$ (the yellow line) and the underlying $\textbf{equilibrium state}$ (the max-entropy curve). A first order phase transition would not necessarily present as a disconnected training trajectory. Instead, its defining feature would be a $\textbf{discontinuous jump in the equilibrium max-entropy curve}$. We would observe the memorization and generalization phases as two distinct, high-entropy regions separated by a low-entropy barrier. 

If grokking was a discontinuous first order transition, reducing the step size (learning rate) would not make it continuous. A smaller LR only shrinks the steps that model takes along training trajectory, but cannot erase the gap if it exists. 

Finally, a low LR does not necessarily prevent grokking. In fact, previous work has found that larger learning rates can sometimes help eliminate grokking [Lv et al., 2024, Language]. This is also consistent with our glass relaxation analogy, because a larger LR is more likely to provide the system with enough "energy" to escape from the low-entropy memorization state.

$\textbf{Q8}$. This task is unlearnable because the training data is insufficient to uniquely determine the underlying rule and is also consistent with with the original work on grokking (Ref [8]).

$\textbf{Q9}$. The training curve in Figure 1b is corresponding to Figure 5b in the Appendix. The initial horizontal movement (memorization) is rapid and takes ~50 epochs. The subsequent vertical ascent (grokking) is much slower and takes ~2000 epochs. 

$\textbf{Q10}$. We thank the reviewer for this feedback and we agree that introducing the ‘conical degree’ concept in the conclusion may lead to potential confusion. Our intention was to provide a brief geometric intuition for why Boltzmann entropy (solution volume) is a more comprehensive measure for generalization than local flatness. As it is not a formal result, we will $\textbf{remove it}$ from the final version to improve clarity.

$\textbf{Q11}$. This is a great question that gets to the core of our analogy, the separation of timescales. For a physical glass, the initial rapid cooling is a fast process, but the subsequent structural relaxation from the initial glassy state to the stable ideal glass state is extremely slow. In grokking, the initial training is like the cooling to a memorization state with near-zero training loss. The network is then kinetically trapped, as the small gradient provides little ‘force’ for large updates. The network can only find the generalization state (ideal glass) via the cumulation of many small stochastic updates, which takes a long time.

$\textbf{Q12}$.  Yes, we checked the gradient norm during the AdamW training and the results support our hypothesis. During the initial memorization phase, the gradient norm is large (>1e-1). However, once the training loss is minimized, the gradient norm drops to an extremely small value (\~1e-7) and remains small during grokking. The drop in gradient norm is the mechanism of the kinetically trapped state, because it leaves the optimizer with little signal to make large updates.

$\textbf{Nits}$. We will edit L177 and L178 in our final version. We also agree with the reviewer that the term ‘relaxation’ may confuse readers unfamiliar with its meaning in physics and will add clarification to section 2.

We also thank the reviewer for the highly relevant suggestion and will cite [Liu et al. 2022 Towards] in the final version. Their finding that a fast-learning decoder can help trigger grokking supports our analogy, as the fast decoder acts as the ‘fast cooling’ that traps the network in a glassy memorization state.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and for recognizing our work's novelty and the paper's clarity. Below we provide our response on a point-by-point basis, to address the reviewer's concerns and improve our manuscript.

$\textbf{Weakness}$

$\textbf{W1. The presentations of WLMD and WanD lacks details}$. We agree that a more intuitive explanation of our core algorithms would be helpful for a broad audience and will add the following clarifications, including new algorithm boxes, to the final version of paper (section 3 and 5 respectively). Our attached code can also serve as a reference if needed. 

$\textbf{WLMD}$: We explain the implementation of WLMD in section 3 and provide the reference of WLMD (Ref [29]) in the main text, which contains the detailed formula derivation. We will incorporate the following explanation to it in the final version.

The key idea behind WLMD is it can avoid getting trapped. Unlike standard samplers that oversample the high entropy regions, it can achieve a uniform sample across all regions of the entropy diagram after convergence. This is realized by maintaining a running estimate of the entropy landscape, which adds an ‘entropy gradient’ to push it from the already-visited states. 

$\textbf{WanD}$: Equation 7 gives the core dynamics of WanD, and we will add the following explanation around it in the final version.

The intuition behind WanD is to utilize the entropy landscape to train models more effectively. It employs 1D WLMD to sample the entropy of training loss and promote exploration of high-entropy regions. This allows WanD to navigate away from the low entropy memorization state, and therefore eliminate the grokking process and finally find high-entropy solutions. We also have an entropy bias (defined in Equation 6) in WanD, which encourages exploration of the low-loss regions.

$\textbf{W2. WanD's Complexity}$. We thank the reviewer for their interest in our toy optimizer, WanD. We reported its computational expense in Appendix A2 together with the details of our experimental configuration but recognize that we did not highlight it clearly in the main text. We will update section 3 in the final version to present it. 
The WanD optimizer is actually quite efficient based on our test on the modular addition task. It needs a similar number of optimization steps (\~2000) to reach generalization, compared with AdamW with the same learning rate (3e-3 for results presented in Figure 3a and 3d). We have also run another experiment with a learning rate of 7e-3 and got similar results (both generalize at \~1400 steps). The running time for WanD is even shorter, which is ~50 seconds per 1K steps (\~72 seconds for AdamW).

$\textbf{Questions}$

$\textbf{Q1}$. We thank the reviewer for this question, and we agree that the "conical degree" concept was not sufficiently explained and could be confusing. Our intention was to provide a high-level geometric intuition of the generalized solution. Our goal was to suggest why Boltzmann entropy (solution volume) is a more comprehensive measure for generalization, compared with the local flatness alone. 

Considering that the ‘conical degree’ is not a formal result of our paper, we will remove it from the final version and only discuss that entropy is a more comprehensive measure since it reflects volume.

$\textbf{Q2}$.  We thank the reviewer for this important question. The continuity of the max-entropy curve in Figure 1 is supported by the primary signature of a continuous transition: the absence of a low entropy barrier. The entropy landscape we finally get is smooth and only has one connected high-entropy region bridging the memorization and generalization states.

In case the reviewer is asking about the finite size effect of neural networks studied, we would like to clarify the scope of our work. Our objective is to study the finite-width networks that are used in practice, rather than infer properties of the infinite-width networks. Therefore, our conclusions cannot be extrapolated to the theoretical infinite-width limit.

$\textbf{Q3}$. We appreciate this insightful question. While a direct empirical comparison is a quite interesting area for future work, we can offer a conceptual comparison between our approach and optimizers like Entropy-SGD, which also leverage the idea of entropy.

The key distinctions are:

$\textbf{- Different entropy}$: The primary difference lies in the definition of entropy. WanD targets the global Boltzmann entropy, which measures the total volume of the solution space. In contrast, Entropy-SGD targets local entropy, a measure of the flatness of a specific minimum. 

$\textbf{- Different methodologies}$: WanD computes entropy via 1D WLMD sampling, whereas Entropy-SGD uses Langevin dynamics to estimate the local entropy gradients.  

$\textbf{Regarding grokking}$: Optimizers like Adam progress slowly due to the insufficient gradient motivation for memorization-to-generalization transitions (Ref [10]). In principle, Entropy-SGD may accelerate grokking if its identified high local-entropy states can generalize. We believe a rigorous empirical comparison remains an excellent direction for future research.

$\textbf{Q4}$. This is an excellent question about the robustness of our findings. As the reviewer observed, symmetry exists between training and test datasets. Therefore, a change in the formula of the training loss is equivalent to a change of the test loss. 

The results in our manuscript use the "smoothed test accuracy": the inverse of which can be considered as a type of loss function. We have internally also experimented with the cross-entropy test loss, instead of the smoothed accuracy. The resulting entropy diagram leads to similar conclusions: there is no entropy barrier and only one connected high-entropy region, providing no evidence of a first order phase transition. This suggests our conclusions are robust given the specific choice of loss function. We will add a note about this to the Appendix in the final version.

We also agree with the reviewer that expanding our analysis to a wider range of grokking-like tasks is an important direction for future work. One such example is using the same task and model design reported in Ref [1], which concludes grokking is a first order transition but uses a slightly different definition of the grokking phenomenon, focusing on the 'sharp drop in test loss' (see Figure 5 in Ref [1]).

$\textbf{W2. Computational Complexity and Feasibility.}$ We thank the reviewer for this important point. We reported the computational cost in Appendix A2 together with the details of our experimental configuration but recognize that we did not highlight it clearly in the main text. We will update section 3 in the final version to clearly present it.

While the computational cost to obtain the converged entropy landscape of this transformer model (with more than $\textbf{400 thousand parameters}$) is relatively high, we believe this analysis itself represents a significant advancement. To the best of our knowledge, the WLMD method is the $\textbf{most efficient}$ entropy sampling algorithm available now, because other methods are limited to models with only hundreds of parameters (as explained by Ref [2]). Besides, considering it takes us ~10,000 NVIDIA 4090 GPU hours to obtain the converged entropy landscape shown in Figure 2 with parallel computation, and that the computational complexity scales linearly with the number of parameters, it is also computationally feasible to scale this work to larger models with tens of millions of parameters if more advanced hardware is available. 

$\textbf{W3. Clarity for Non-Physicists.}$ We agree with the reviewer that our manuscript uses some physics terminology, like thermodynamic equilibrium, glass relaxation, and Boltzmann entropy. This is mainly  due to its nature as a statistical physics inspired work. We defined and explained these concepts when we mentioned them and will also utilize the additional page allowance in the final version to add more intuitive analogies to ensure the work is self-contained for a broad audience. We also welcome the reviewer to suggest specific concepts that may need additional clarification and we will supplement them in the final version. 

$\textbf{W4. Missing or Understated Insights.}$ We thank the reviewer for highlighting the connection to prior work as a strength of our study. Due to the length limitations, we only have a section to briefly discuss these connections at the end of the manuscript. We will add an additional appendix to discuss more details in the final version. The reviewer’s reasoning about the underlying mechanism of the connection between high entropy solution and learned sparse structure / representation shift is also precise. Therefore, below we detailed it as an example of the explanation we will add.

Ref [24] has shown that grokking is related to sparse subnetworks, where only a few neurons participate in the memorization of the rules. From our entropy perspective, for the NN with this generalized sparse subnetwork, since the parameters outside the sparse subnetwork do not contribute to the generalizability, their perturbation would not harm generalization. Therefore, they constitute a solution set with a larger volume in the parameter space. The entropy of this solution set is defined as the logarithm of the volume in the parameter space. Thus, the entropy of the NN with sparse subnetworks is larger.

$\textbf{Q1.}$ We are encouraged by the reviewer's interest in WanD and would like to provide more experimental details about it below.
 
$\textbf{- Efficiency}$: Due to the scope of this work, we only tested WanD on the modular addition task. Compared with AdamW with the same learning rate (3e-3 for results presented in Figure 3a and 3d), they need a similar number of optimization steps (\~2000) to reach generalization. We have also run another experiment with a learning rate of 7e-3 and got similar results (both generalize at \~1400 steps). As a WLMD-based algorithm, we acknowledge that there are many hyperparameters that need to be set. Our experiments find that the learning rate, temperature, and friction coefficient are the $\textbf{three key factors}$ that determine the training results.

summary.value: This paper presents a novel interpretation of the grokking phenomenon in neural networks through the lens of statistical physics, particularly computational glass relaxation. It employs the Wang-Landau Molecular Dynamics algorithm to estimate entropy landscapes in modular arithmetic tasks and demonstrates that grokking does not correspond to a first-order phase transition, contradicting prior work. Additionally, the authors propose a physics-inspired optimizer, WanD, capable of eliminating grokking without explicit regularization.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1. Novel Theoretical Perspective: The paper provides a fresh and compelling physical analogy for an AI phenomenon. Viewing a neural network as a physical system and grokking as analogous to glass transition/relaxation is an innovative framing. This perspective synthesizes ideas from statistical mechanics with deep learning, potentially opening new avenues for understanding generalization. The analogy is well-grounded in the results: the authors show that pre-grokking fast training is analogous to rapidly quenching a liquid into a glass (a non-equilibrium state), and the grokking phase is akin to a slow structural relaxation toward equilibrium.

2. Entropy Landscape Analysis: Methodologically, the use of the Wang-Landau Molecular Dynamics algorithm to sample the entropy landscape of neural network parameters is a significant strength. This approach goes beyond conventional training-loss landscapes by explicitly estimating the Boltzmann entropy (volume of solutions) at different performance levels. The paper thus moves beyond local geometry (sharpness or flatness of minima) to a global thermodynamic view of the parameter space.

3. Connection to Prior Work: The authors do a good job situating their contribution relative to prior explanations of grokking. They explicitly discuss how their entropy-based view can account for earlier observations.  At the same time, they challenge two prominent prior hypotheses – the phase transition interpretation and the weight-norm-driven explanation.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited Scope of Experiments: A notable limitation is that all experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale, synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic problems with a small transformer). 

2. Computational Complexity and Feasibility: The approach of sampling an entropy landscape with WLMD, while powerful, is computationally intensive and may not be practical beyond toy settings. The paper does not clearly report the computational cost of obtaining the entropy landscape for even these small models.

3. Clarity for Non-Physicists: The paper assumes a certain comfort with physics terminology which might pose a barrier to some readers.

4. Missing or Understated Insights: The paper touches on how its findings relate to earlier hypotheses (like representation learning or the slingshot effect), but these connections remain somewhat abstract. For example, it is asserted that the entropy perspective can explain observations of representation shift or sparse subnetworks, yet the reader must infer the mechanism (presumably, high-entropy solutions correspond to learned sparse structures or improved features). These connections would be more convincing if explicitly demonstrated or at least elaborated.

summary.value:
This work draws an analogy between
grokking in neural networks (a sudden drop in test error 
well after the network has memorized the training data) 
and the behavior of particles in a liquid after
a sudden temperature drop. 
Building on this connection, the authors construct a phase
diagram of the entropy (volume of weight configurations) of a one-layer transformer with a given training loss and test accuracy. 
They observe that:
1) in the grokking regime (low training loss), the entropy
landscape does not exhibit any barrier, challenging the 
belief that grokking is a first-order phase transition;
2) the solutions that maximize the entropy 
for a fixed training loss generalize well and do not 
exhibit grokking.

Based on these insights, the authors introduce a new 
algorithm that targets high-entropy solutions and avoids grokking without 
the need to control weight norms.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strengths

1. This is a very interesting contribution to the
    ongoing discussion around the origin of grokking.
2. Overall, the paper is cleanly written, the story
    is clear and the experimental results are well presented.

## Weaknesses

1. The presentation of the two core algorithms
    (for the simulation of the entropy landscape and targeting high-entropy solutions)
    lack details, both in terms of how and why they
    work, and how they were implemented. It would
    be helpful to give more intuition on
    them, especially for a broader
    ML audience, which is unlikely to be familiar with
    Wang-Landau molecular dynamics.
2. My understanding is that 
    the proposed WandD algorithm is computationally expensive. A discussion about its complexity/convergence rate 
    would strengthen the work.

questions.value:
1. I found the intuition behind the notion of
    ''conical degree'' in Section 6 somewhat confusing.
    Is there a specific reason to believe that the cutoff
    induced by fixing the training loss admits a simple
    geometric interpretation?
2. Figure 1.(b) seems to be the key experimental
    result, as this is where grokking is most apparent for AdamW. The max-entropy curve in this panel
    appears to rise sharply towards perfect test accuracy. How did you ensure that the continuity of the 
    max-entropy curve is not a finite-size effect?
3. Several algorithms have been proposed to explicitly target high-entropy solutions in the traditional loss landscape sense (for example https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-5468/ab39d9). How do those methods compare empirically to the one proposed in this paper, both in terms of generalization performance and existence of grokking?
4. In the sampling of the entropy landscape using molecular dynamics (Equation 4), the training loss and test error appear to play symmetric roles, especially in the absence of regularization in the training loss. This makes me wonder, how robust are the resulting phase diagrams to changes in the choice of training loss?

summary.value:
- Authors compare grokking to a slow relaxation of a many-body system into an equilibrium state after a rapid cooling process
- they argue against a first-order state transition interpretation, as brought forward by previous work, by investigating the boltzmann entropy landscape as a function of train loss and test accuracy and finding no discontinuity in the order parameter during the transition process
- authors argue for a “high entropy advantage” in the grokking scenario. The training trajectory in the (train loss, test acc) landscape differs vastly from a more beneficial trajectory, the maximum entropy curve, which achieves high test accuracy much quicker. they claim a broad correlation between high (boltzmann) entropy solutions and generalizability in neural networks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths

- quite clean experiments with nice interpretations
- interesting hypothesis and theory
- a refreshing perspective on grokking

Weaknesses

- the binning in (train loss, test acc) seems somewhat arbitrary. I understand that it is necessary for the simulation and the calculation of $S$, but I can imagine that different binning schemes can have vastly different outcomes if the landscape is not very regular. How do you account for that?
- the impact of this work is not super clear to me. while it is an interesting hypothesis and seems to have some confirming evidence, what should I take away from this for the general community? the entropy to generalization link is certainly broadly interesting, but that contribution belongs to [2]. I am not convinced about the utility of the WanD optimizer.
- there should be a proof (or at least a link to one) that the WLMD sampling converges to the true $S$ at the places where it is sampled. There are so many possible parameter configurations that it sounds non-trivial to get a grasp of true entropy by iterating this algorithm.
- the authors claim to overthrow the first-order transition hypothesis from Rubin  et al [1] and attribute the differences to data and training setup. It seems weird that they don’t attempt the same setup as [1] to see whether they reach the same conclusion there, since they claim the disproving of [1] as a main contribution.

questions.value:
- What the relationship between $U$ and $(L_{train}, A_{test})$ ?
- I don’t really understand the WL simulation. How exactly is $\frac{\partial S}{\partial L_{train}}$ calculated? You say via numerical differentiation of adjacent bins, but that estimate is very bad at the beginning of the simulation right? Don’t you need to sample a lot of parameter configurations to estimate that? Maybe a proof of how it converges to the right estimate would be helpful.
- Also a little algorithm box explaining the exact steps to simulate and update NN parameters would be helpful.
- Why do you need to conserve kinetic energy? Otherwise updates become too large as potential energy is transferred into kinetic?
- you conclude that grokking is not a first order phase transition because you don’t see a discontinuity in the order parameter you choose (test accuracy). Does that mean that no order parameter that one could choose would be discontinuous?
- why does the need to cross a free-energy barrier imply a first order phase transition? because crossing wouldn’t happen unless one jumps right to the other side, implying a discontinuity (like quantum tunneling)?
- How would a discontinuity present itself in Fig 1? Would the yellow line be disconnected?
    - If that is the case, could one not always reduce the size of the update (i.e. learning rate) to make it continuous? Or would grokking just never appear with such a low learning rate in that view?
- Why can Fig 1(c) not be learned by training?
- How much of the training time in Fig 1(b) goes into the vertical ascent of the yellow curve vs the horizontal move along the train loss?
- how does the conical degree combine weight norm and flatness? it would help to expand a little on that, it’s a little weird to introduce this notion in the conclusion.
- i don’t understand why the glassy interpretation implies that generalization takes a long time.
- do you actually check the gradient norms during the relaxation process to corroborate your hypothesis?

Nits:

- L177 define A_test and L_train
- L178: calculates → calculate
- I was confused by the term “relaxation” until the very end (L354), expecting some relaxation of constraints as is common in optimization. maybe explain in the beginning that you call it relaxation because of the term “structural relaxation”.

limitations.value:
consider citing and discussing the relationship to https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10343v2

overall I like the view this paper takes, but there are some holes in explanation and experimental and theoretical rigor. I am willing to adjust my score if my weaknesses and questions are addressed to my satisfaction.

summary.value: This work investigates, from a theoretical point of view, the grokking phase in NNs. The analysis is recast as a physical system modelled by computational glass relaxation, where the parameters are degrees of freedom, and energy is the corresponding training loss. This approach enables the authors to associate the memorization process with the rapid cooling of a liquid into a non-equilibrium state and the subsequent generalization with the slow relaxation towards stability. In this setup, one can define the NN Bolzman entropy. Experiments are conducted using transformers on modulo arithmetic tasks and reveal the connections between high-entropy minima and generalization ability. A novel toy optimizer that can avoid grokking is presented as a practical outcome of the previous analysis.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value: The paper introduces a compelling and original perspective by modeling grokking as a computational analog of glass relaxation. This physical analogy helps explain the delayed generalization phase in neural networks, using entropy landscape analysis to challenge the prevailing interpretation of grokking as a first-order phase transition. The proposed optimizer (WanD) envisions the potential practical impact of the study. More experiments with Wand could be added to support the theoretical findings.

questions.value:
I list some minor concerns:
- (pag. 4) Is there any limitation in constraining the NN parameters to the range $3 / \sqrt m$? 
- (pag. 4) It is stated that in Sec. 4.2  the weight norm is limited to 30. How is this enforced during training without impacting the learning dynamic?
- In Sect. 5, WanD is tested only on the modular addition $p=67$ task that exhibits the grokking phase. Nonetheless, it would be important to add at least one experiment without grokking to ensure that WanD can be used in a general training setup when the nature of the task to be solved is unknown in advance.

limitations.value: The limitation section is missing. I think it is important to add a discussion on the current limitations of the study worked out on toy modular arithmetic tasks with one-layer transformer.

title.value: Is Grokking a Computational Glass Relaxation?

TLDR.value: By framing grokking as computational glass relaxation, this work explains grokking from the perspective of Boltzmann entropy and proposes a physics-based grokking-resistant optimizer.

abstract.value:
Understanding neural network' (NN) generalizability remains a central question in deep learning research.
The special phenomenon of grokking, where NNs abruptly generalize long after the training performance reaches near-perfect level, offers a unique window to investigate the underlying mechanisms of NNs' generalizability.
Here we propose an interpretation for grokking by framing it as a computational glass relaxation: viewing NNs as a physical system where parameters are the degrees of freedom and train loss is the system energy, we find memorization process resembles a rapid cooling of liquid into non-equilibrium glassy state at low temperature and the later generalization is like a slow relaxation towards a more stable configuration. 
This mapping enables us to sample NNs' Boltzmann entropy (states of density) landscape as a function of training loss and test accuracy. 
Our experiments in transformers on arithmetic tasks suggests that there is NO entropy barrier in the memorization-to-generalization transition of grokking, challenging previous theory that defines grokking as a first-order phase transition.
We identify a high-entropy advantage under grokking, an extension of prior work linking entropy to generalizability but much more significant. 
Inspired by grokking's far-from-equilibrium nature, we develop a toy optimizer WanD based on Wang-landau molecular dynamics, which can eliminate grokking without any constraints and find high-norm generalizing solutions. 
This provides strictly-defined counterexamples to theory attributing grokking solely to weight norm evolution towards the Goldilocks zone and also suggests new potential ways for optimizer design.
